overview: Compass Group is the world's largest contract catering and food services company, providing outsourced food services and targeted support services (cleaning, facilities, reception) to clients across North America and International (Europe, Asia Pacific, Rest of World) markets. The Group operates through five client sectors - Business & Industry, Healthcare & Senior Living, Education, Sports & Leisure, and Defence, Offshore & Remote - using a portfolio of bespoke, decentralised B2B brands rather than a single consumer brand. Fiscal year ends 30 September; Compass switched its primary reporting currency from GBP to USD effective FY2024, and from 1 April 2026 also changed the trading currency of its LSE-listed shares from sterling to US dollars.

business_model.summary: Compass earns multi-year contract fees from clients (corporations, hospitals, universities, stadiums, defence/resource operators) to run on-site catering and support services, typically on a cost-plus-management-fee or profit-and-loss basis; growth compounds through organic like-for-like growth (pricing plus volume), net new business wins (4-5% annual target), and bolt-on/platform M&A. Revenue is largely contractual and recurring (multi-year contracts, high ~96% client retention) rather than one-off/project based, giving strong visibility.
business_model.customer_type: B2B, long-term outsourcing contracts with large employers, healthcare/senior living operators, universities/schools, stadiums/venues, and defence/energy/mining clients
business_model.geographic_mix: North America ~68% of underlying revenue, International (Europe, Asia Pacific, Rest of World, combined from FY2025) ~32%

competitive_position.market_position: Global #1 in contract catering/food services with roughly 11-15% share of a highly fragmented ~$360bn addressable global food services market (management estimate); larger than Sodexo ($26bn revenue) and Aramark ($18.5bn revenue) combined on revenue. Nearly three-quarters of the addressable market remains self-operated or served by small regional/local players, giving Compass a long structural runway via first-time outsourcing (around half of new business wins in recent periods).

moat_factors.description: Global purchasing scale lets Compass negotiate better food and supply costs than in-house operators and smaller rivals, and better absorb food/labour inflation; Group Purchasing Organisations now run in five of its top ten markets.
~96% client retention; multi-year contracts, embedded operational integration (staffing, menus, systems) and reputational/food-safety risk of switching providers create high switching costs.

Decentralised structure with bespoke sector-specific brands (vs. one-size-fits-all) lets Compass tailor offerings to Business & Industry, Healthcare, Education, Sports & Leisure, and Defence/Offshore clients, a differentiator versus generalist competitors.
Above-unit overhead leverage improves as revenue scales within a region/sector, supporting margin progression (underlying operating margin up from ~6.8% in FY2022 to 7.2% in FY2025).

Strong investment-grade credit ratings (S&P A/A-1, Moody's A2/P-1) support continued bolt-on M&A and give risk-averse clients confidence in long-term service continuity, a differentiator versus smaller or private-equity-owned rivals.
Investment in digital ordering, cashierless payments and AI-enabled operations supports retention and new wins, including servicing AI hyperscaler data centre construction/operations sites.

weaknesses: Thin absolute margins (underlying operating margin ~7.2%) leave limited room for execution error given high labour and food cost intensity
Heavy reliance on North America (~68% of revenue) concentrates currency and macro exposure
Labour-intensive model (over 590,000 employees) exposed to wage inflation and talent/attrition risk
Fragmented competitive landscape means constant re-tendering risk even with high retention
Integration risk from an accelerating pace of bolt-on and platform M&A (Vermaat, Dupont Restauration, 4Service, Pro Care Management)

growth_drivers: Organic revenue growth from net new business wins sustained in the 4-5% target range for five consecutive years (vs. ~3% pre-pandemic), plus pricing and like-for-like volume growth

First-time outsourcing: roughly half of new business wins come from clients outsourcing food/support services for the first time, within an addressable market still ~75% self-operated or served by regional players
Bolt-on and platform M&A, especially building a European growth platform (Dupont Restauration, 4Service, Vermaat, Pro Care Management) replicating the successful North America M&A playbook
Secular structural outsourcing trend as clients face rising regulatory, food-safety, cost and talent complexity
Growing exposure to high-growth niches: AI/hyperscaler data centre construction and operations catering, defence and energy infrastructure investment, and under-penetrated Sports & Leisure venues
Ongoing underlying operating margin progression from overhead leverage, procurement scale and M&A synergies
Total addressable market estimated to grow at ~5% per annum, from ~$360bn now toward a management estimate of ~$600bn by 2035
Capital returned to shareholders via progressive dividend and opportunistic share buybacks ($2.3bn returned since 2022)

business.description: Although retention is ~96%, the business depends on continually winning and retaining large numbers of discrete client contracts in a competitive, fragmented market; loss of major contracts or failure to meet contractual service levels can trigger claims or revenue loss.

Reliance on hundreds of thousands of front-line staff; attracting, retaining and motivating workers at all levels is flagged as a principal risk, particularly amid wage inflation and tight labour markets.

Feeding millions of consumers daily; safety breaches could cause business interruption, litigation, and reputational damage; occupational safety breaches carry similar risk given the scale of the workforce.
No single client dominates revenue, but North America represents ~68% of Group revenue, concentrating exposure to US corporate real estate/return-to-office trends and US healthcare/education funding.

financial.description: Net debt rose to $6.4bn (1.4x net debt/underlying EBITDA at FY2025) after heavy bolt-on and platform M&A spend (Vermaat alone $1.7-1.9bn); leverage covenant and interest cover tested semi-annually, policy target range 1.0-1.5x.
UK defined benefit plan surplus reduced to $327m (from $542m) and rest-of-Group schemes carry a net deficit of $125m, requiring ongoing funding and monitoring.
Policy fixes/caps at least 80% of projected debt for year one, tapering to 0-40% hedged in years four+, leaving some exposure to rate moves on unhedged tranches.

regulatory.risk: Food safety and labour regulation across 25+ countries
regulatory.description: Operates under varying food hygiene, allergen, and workplace safety regimes; non-compliance risks fines, litigation and reputational damage.

Operates numerous legacy subsidiaries, some in low-tax jurisdictions; diverging tax authority interpretations on cross-border transactions create ongoing tax risk and uncertainty, though Compass states it does not use tax havens to avoid tax.
Accelerating bolt-on and platform acquisitions (e.g., Vermaat) require regulatory approval and could draw increased competition authority scrutiny as Compass consolidates fragmented markets.

macro.description: Multi-currency operations (USD reporting since FY2024, GBP dividends, EUR/GBP debt) create translation volatility; FX swung operating profit and net debt materially in FY2025 (e.g., $171m FX loss on net debt translation); the April 2026 switch of LSE trading currency to USD reduces share-price FX noise for US-centric reporting but GBP/USD moves still affect UK-domiciled shareholders and reported sterling dividends.

Food costs are roughly one-third of costs and labour makes up the bulk of in-unit costs; c.$1 billion of additional food costs noted in FY2025; cost indexation clauses partially offset this via contractual pricing rights, but inflation volatility and economic downturns remain a principal risk.

Volumes in Business & Industry (largest sector) are tied to office attendance/corporate headcount; economic slowdowns can reduce discretionary catering spend and volumes, though contract-based, multi-year revenue provides some resilience versus pure discretionary consumer spend.

Middle East conflict and Russia-Ukraine war flagged as elevating economic volatility and cyber-security threat; Compass has exited Russia and does not operate in Israel/Palestinian territories but has limited Middle East interests.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Global outsourced food services market estimated by management at ~$360bn, growing ~5% per year, with a long-term ambition of ~$600bn by 2035; nearly three-quarters of the market remains self-operated or served by small regional players, implying a long structural outsourcing runway for scale players like Compass.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderately defensive - multi-year B2B contracts and recurring revenue provide resilience versus pure discretionary consumer spending, but volumes in Business & Industry and Sports & Leisure have some sensitivity to corporate occupancy, consumer footfall and event calendars.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Low-to-moderate - mostly fixed/hedged debt (80%+ of near-term projected debt fixed or capped), but rising net debt from accelerated M&A increases finance costs sensitivity over time.
key_input_costs: Food and ingredient costs (~1/3 of costs)
Labour costs (majority of in-unit costs, >590,000 employees)

recent_developments.event: FY2025 organic revenue growth of 8.7%, underlying operating margin up 10bps to 7.2%, underlying operating profit up 11.7% constant currency to $3,335m; client retention improved to 96.3%; completed exits from Chile, Colombia, Mexico and Kazakhstan, concluding the strategic portfolio review.

Agreed to acquire Vermaat Groep B.V. in the Netherlands for an enterprise value of ~EUR1.5bn (~$1.7-1.9bn) from Bridgepoint, Compass's largest European deal to date, extending the North America M&A playbook into Europe.
Completed the Vermaat acquisition for $1.7bn, strengthening positions in the Netherlands, France and Germany.

Q1 FY2026 trading update: organic revenue growth 7.3%, net new business within 4-5% target; announced intention to change LSE share trading currency from GBP to USD effective 1 April 2026 to align with USD financial reporting and reduce FX noise in the share price (dividends remain payable in sterling unless shareholders elect USD); FY2026 guidance reaffirmed at ~10% underlying operating profit growth.
LSE trading currency for Compass ordinary shares switched from GBP to USD; no change to FTSE index inclusion or LSE listing.

H1 revenue +9% to $25.0bn, underlying operating profit +12% (constant currency) to $1.84bn, underlying operating margin up 20bps to 7.4%; organic revenue growth 7.2% with 96% client retention; acquired Pro Care Management in Germany for $270m; raised FY2026 underlying operating profit growth guidance from ~10% to above 11%; interim dividend raised 13% to 25.5c.

Organic revenue growth 7.1% in the quarter; net new business wins over the trailing 12 months reached $4.3bn, up 16% year-on-year, with 50% from first-time outsourcing; reiterated FY2026 guidance of above 11% underlying operating profit growth; noted growing exposure to AI hyperscaler data centre construction/operations catering and a record Education selling season (University of Kentucky, largest Education win to date).
Governance: Stefan Bomhard to retire from the Board at the 2026 AGM after nine years; Liat Ben-Zur and Juliana Chugg (appointed 2024) completed induction and continue as directors.

items.notes: Raised from 'around 10%' guided at Q1 FY2026 to 'above 11%' at H1 FY2026 results and reiterated at Q3; driven by ~7% organic revenue growth, ~2% profit growth from M&A, and ongoing margin progression.
Q3 YTD actual organic growth running at 7.2%, Q3 standalone at 7.1%, in line with guidance; net new business growth within the 4-5% target range for a fifth consecutive year.
Reflects Vermaat and Pro Care Management integration.

items.target: ~3.5% of sales (full-year), trending slightly above FY2025's 3.3%
items.notes: Q3 update noted capex running ~3.5% of sales YTD and expected to be 'slightly elevated' at full year due to timing of client mobilisations.
Reiterated alongside 'ongoing margin progression' and 'profit growth ahead of revenue growth' as the long-term growth algorithm.
Stood at 1.4x at FY2025 year-end after Vermaat-related M&A spend; policy to maintain strong investment-grade ratings.
FY2025 dividend of 65.9c/share, up 10.2%; H1 FY2026 interim dividend raised 13% to 25.5c, consistent with policy.

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Dominic Blakemore highlighted 'the strongest pipeline of opportunities we have ever seen,' citing market share gains across multiple sectors and confidence in 'another year of strong earnings growth and continued margin progression' given the >$360bn addressable market. Management flagged capex running slightly above plan due to client mobilisation timing but reiterated full-year guidance at the Q3 update, with M&A spend ($2.4bn YTD through Q3) broadly unchanged from the half-year level.

bull_case: Structural outsourcing tailwind: ~75% of the ~$360bn addressable market remains self-operated or served by regional players, giving Compass a long multi-year runway via first-time outsourcing wins

Consistent execution track record: net new business growth sustained in the 4-5% target range for five consecutive years with client retention near/above 96%, evidencing a durable competitive moat in scale, sectorisation and procurement

Margin and earnings momentum: underlying operating margin has expanded from ~6.8% (FY2022) to 7.4% (H1 FY2026), with FY2026 operating profit guidance raised twice this year to 'above 11%' growth, well ahead of revenue growth

Disciplined, well-funded M&A optionality: strong investment-grade balance sheet (leverage 1.0-1.5x target) funds bolt-on and platform M&A (Vermaat, Pro Care Management) replicating a proven North America playbook in a newly-created European growth platform

Exposure to new secular demand pools, including catering for AI/hyperscaler data centre construction and operations sites, defence/energy infrastructure investment, and under-penetrated Sports & Leisure venues
Shareholder-friendly capital allocation: progressive dividend (~50% payout) plus opportunistic buybacks ($2.3bn returned since 2022) alongside reinvestment for growth
bear_case: Thin absolute operating margins (~7%) in a labour- and food-cost-intensive, people-heavy business leave limited buffer against wage or input cost inflation shocks

Rising leverage from an accelerating M&A pace (net debt up to $6.4bn, 1.4x EBITDA at FY2025, with further Vermaat/Pro Care-related spend in FY2026) increases integration and financial risk if growth slows
Heavy North America concentration (~68% of revenue) ties results closely to US corporate occupancy trends, healthcare/education funding, and USD strength/weakness

Multi-currency complexity (recent GBP-to-USD reporting switch and LSE trading currency change) can create FX translation volatility in reported results and may confuse year-on-year comparability for some investors during the transition period

Highly competitive, fragmented market (Sodexo, Aramark, Elior, ISS, and in-house/self-operated catering) means constant re-tender risk despite high retention, and new disruptive/technology-enabled entrants are explicitly flagged as a principal risk

Valuation already reflects strong execution (consensus BUY-leaning, but a wide analyst target range of roughly GBP32.6-56.2 suggests meaningful disagreement on fair value), raising the bar for continued outperformance
